to fly with an old experienced pilot and criticise his handling
of the plane, or his navigation, without incurring a certain
amount of resentment.
But these pilots have accepted my suggestions
and criticism cheerfully and have assisted our work to the limit

visibilitywas less than a mile. Then he turned to come back. At
that moment the haze was probably fairly thick, and while he might
have seen an island or hill in plenty of time to avoid it he could'nt
hee f0g. He had the misfortune to come out of his turn at the edge
of & local log bank that surrounded a high island. He did not see
the fog bank and he flew right into it, and struck the island an
instant later.
I do not for a moment deny that the cresh was avoidable, but
in my judgement it was excusable under the conditions that prevailed.
Undoubtedly the pilot was endeavouring to use his best judgement.
It i8 fairly evident that his judgement must have been at fault as
to the amount of visibility available. With a visibility of a mile
he should certainly have been able to detect fog before running into
it, therefore we reason that his visibility must have been conside-
rably less than a mile. But the usual facilities available to a
pilot for checking visibility were lacking in this case.
I therefore
do not feel that it would be fair or correct to say that the pilot
deliberately proceeded in weather which he knew offered less than
a mile of visibility.
Rumill is as careful and conservative a pilot as I have ever
known.
He is incapable of a, lie and has made no attempt to alibi
himselt out of any possible blame. He will remain grounded until
you cable us your decision.
My own recommendation is that he be reinstated in our service.
Every passenger from the crash has expressed an admiration for him
and for his actions during and immediately after the crash, and
have publicly stated their desire to fly with him again.
I sincerely hope you will not think me unduly sympathetic in
this case.
It I felt that Rumill had deliberately broken our
safety rules, and thereby risked the lives of passengers in his care,
I should testify to that effect, were he my own brother. As a matter
of fact, it ls difficult for me to avoid a tendency to blame Rumi1l
more than he deserves, for the reason that the effect of this crash
is so destructive to our plans and hopes. We had the entire
confidence of the public from here to Menila, as well as their strong
interest and goodwill. Now we have lost a lot of that.

I have done my very best on this
job, and that I have endeavoured to
make this line as thoroughly Pan Amerlean as is the Caribbean Division

wi11 know that I would not ask you to reinstate Rumill if I did not

been doing Rumill's share of the flying
and it is difficult for me to spare that much time. If you will
